story:
Three big Cedars of Lebanon act as the front door of Square Gustave-Auguste Ferrié. The Métropole's register of remarkable trees, which protects them under Lyon's planning rules, says the group marks the entrance to the square and gives the public garden its identity. Stand at the corner of rue Jacques-Louis Hénon and rue Deleuvre and you are looking at them.

They are best understood as a group rather than three separate trees. A cedar of Lebanon on its own spreads its branches wide and level; three planted together at an entrance make an evergreen gateway that holds its shape through every season, while the deciduous trees elsewhere in the square come and go. That is what the register is protecting, the way the trio frames the place as much as the size of any one trunk.

The register gives no measurements and no planting date for them. Nothing on record dates the group, so this page gives it no age. The register entry was last updated in September 2021, and street-level photographs from the corner run up to 2026.

The square has two more protected entries, three copper beeches and a red oak, so it rewards a slow circuit. If you know when the cedars went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the three big evergreen cedars together at the square's entrance. They stand at the corner of rue Jacques-Louis Hénon and rue Deleuvre in Square Gustave-Auguste Ferrié.

story:
Copper beeches are relatively rare around Lyon, the Métropole's register says, and Square Gustave-Auguste Ferrié has three of them together. The register protects them as a very fine group, remarkable both for their size and for that rarity, at the rue Deleuvre corner of the square.

A copper beech is a beech with purple leaves, and the colour changes through the year. The new leaves open purple in spring, darken through the summer and turn coppery before they fall. Three of them side by side make a block of colour, at its strongest in late April and May when the foliage is fresh.

The register does not say how old these are, and gives no girth or height, so this page leaves the age open rather than guessing.

The register entry was last updated in September 2021, and street-level photographs taken near the corner run into 2026. The same square holds three Cedars of Lebanon at its entrance and a big red oak on the rue Hénon side. If you know how long the beeches have stood here, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by their purple leaves, three beeches together, unlike anything else in the square. They stand at the rue Deleuvre corner of Square Gustave-Auguste Ferrié, near the entrance cedars.

story:
Square Gustave-Auguste Ferrié has an American at its edge. This northern red oak stands at the street edge on rue Jacques-Louis Hénon, and the register of remarkable trees protects it as a very large and very fine specimen, remarkable for its size and for its spread.

That spread is what you notice from the pavement. Planted at the edge of the square, its crown reaches out over the street side as well as the garden. In summer it is simply a big green oak with broad, sharply lobed leaves. In late October and November it changes character, turning a rich red for a few weeks.

Quercus rubra comes from eastern North America and has been planted in European parks for a long time, but the register gives no planting date for this one and no measurements. This page gives it no age and no girth, only what the register says, that it is very large.

The register entry was last updated in September 2021, and street-level photographs near the spot run into 2026. With the three entrance cedars and the three copper beeches a few dozen metres away, the square makes a compact walk of seven protected trees. If you know this oak's age, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the single big oak at the square's street edge, its wide crown reaching over rue Jacques-Louis Hénon, red in autumn. It stands in Square Gustave-Auguste Ferrié.

best_time.label: late October into November, when the leaves turn a rich red

story:
The Métropole's register says trees like this one have become rare in Greater Lyon. It protects a large hickory in the Jardin des Chartreux, in good health, on the slope below the Croix-Rousse that once belonged to the Carthusian monastery the garden is named after.

The register's own label is part of the puzzle. It files the tree as Juglans ovoida, with Hickory in quotation marks and Caryer d'Amérique, American hickory, in French. That Latin mixes the walnut genus with what reads like the shagbark hickory, Carya ovata, and no accepted species carries the name as written. Hickories are close relatives of walnuts, so the slip is easy to understand, but it leaves the exact species open. This page calls it a hickory and asks you. If you can tell a shagbark from its cousins, by its bark or its nuts, let us know which it is.

The register gives no height, girth or planting date, so this page gives it no age. Its entry was last updated in June 2016, and street-level photographs near the garden run to early 2026, though none shows this trunk itself. If you find it, a photograph would settle both questions, where exactly it stands and what it is.

The garden is better known for its magnolias, cedars and horse chestnuts. By the register.s account, the hickory is the rarer find.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the garden's large hickory, a walnut relative, among the magnolias, cedars and horse chestnuts of the Jardin des Chartreux. The garden opens off cours du Général Giraud.

story:
The Métropole calls this cedar very rare, and protects it as a single remarkable tree in the landscape for three reasons, its species, its habit and its amplitude. It is a weeping blue Atlas cedar, the cultivar Glauca Pendula, in Square Henri Dor in Caluire-et-Cuire.

The cultivar is a strange tree to meet. An ordinary Atlas cedar grows up and out in tiers. Glauca Pendula grows blue-grey needles on branches that hang straight down, so that an old one looks less like a conifer than a blue curtain. The register picks this one out for its amplitude, the sheer reach of it, which is what makes it worth crossing into Caluire for.

The register does not record its height, its spread in metres or when it was planted, and nothing else on record dates it, so this page gives it no age. The entry was last updated in October 2023, and street-level photographs near the square run into 2026.

Caluire-et-Cuire sits on the plateau just north of the Croix-Rousse, and the square is in the Bissardon neighbourhood. If you visit, tell us how far its branches now reach, and if you know when it went in, tell us that too.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its blue-grey needles on branches that hang straight down, the weeping form its cultivar name describes. It stands in Square Henri Dor in Caluire-et-Cuire.

story:
The Métropole's register puts these three planes at more than 30 metres tall and more than 150 years old. It protects them along Quai Georges Clemenceau in Caluire-et-Cuire, on the Saône near Le Vernay, as remarkable for both their exceptional size and their age.

Thirty metres is a ten-storey building, three times over in a row along the river. The register does not give a girth, and its figures are words rather than a fresh measurement, so the honest summary is very tall and very old, by the Métropole's own account.

Among the trees on this page, few carry a written age at all. These three do, from the body that protects them.

The caution is about the present rather than the past. The register entry was last updated in October 2023, but the only street-level photographs found at the spot date from August 2020, so recent confirmation is thin. If you walk or cycle along Quai Clemenceau, tell us all three still stand, and send a photograph if you can.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as three planes over 30 metres tall, close together along the roadside of Quai Georges Clemenceau. They stand on the Saône bank near Le Vernay in Caluire-et-Cuire.

story:
Two planes frame the church of Saint-Côme-Saint-Damien at 53 chemin de Fond Rose, and the Métropole protects them for the size of their crowns. The register of remarkable trees names three reasons in all, their crown spread, where they stand and what they add to the landscape.

Position matters here more than for most trees on this page. A church forecourt is a deliberate place, built to be seen and approached, and a pair of wide-crowned planes on it shapes the whole view of the building. The two register points sit about 20 metres apart, close enough to read as a pair from the road.

The register gives no height, no girth and no planting date. Nothing else on record dates them either, so this page gives them no age.

This is the least confirmed entry in Caluire-et-Cuire. The register was last updated in October 2023, and that update is the most recent sign of the trees. No street-level photograph or other recent trace of them has turned up. They may stand exactly as described, but it is fair to say plainly that nobody has shown it lately.

So this is an invitation. If you pass the church on chemin de Fond Rose, tell us whether both planes are still there, and send a photograph if you can.

story:
These two planes have never been pruned since the day they were planted. The Métropole's register of remarkable trees says so in as many words, and adds that a plane grown this way, in its natural shape, is rarely seen anywhere in Greater Lyon.

Most city planes are cut back to fit the street around them, their crowns shaped by whoever last trimmed them. On Rue Pierre Termier in Collonges-au-Mont-d'Or, the register says, the space around these two let them do what a plane does when nobody interferes, and each has built a crown of rare breadth. It calls them very healthy and gives them a long life expectancy still ahead.

That is the reason to come. Not a famous name or a story, but the chance to see what a London plane looks like when it is left alone, two of them about 30 metres apart.

The register gives no height, girth or planting date, so this page gives them no age. Its entry was last updated in September 2021, and street-level photographs at the spot date from October 2022. Collonges is about 12 kilometres up the Saône from central Lyon, near the edge of a comfortable day trip. If you visit, tell us how wide those crowns have grown.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by their crowns, broad and in natural shape, never cut back, on two planes about 30 metres apart. They stand on Rue Pierre Termier in Collonges-au-Mont-d'Or.

The register entry is brief and almost entirely about size. Two very large trees, 35 metres high, in excellent health, and easy to see. The height is the register's own figure rather than a fresh survey, but even with some margin it puts them among the tallest trees on this page.

What the register does not give is everything else. There is no girth, no planting date and no story attached to them, and nothing else on record dates them, so this page gives them no age. They are simply two enormous trees, standing at a community building rather than in a park or a square.

The register entry was last updated in June 2016, but street-level photographs taken nearby run from 2021 to June 2026, so there is good reason to expect them to be standing. If you go, tell us how they look, and if you know when they were planted, tell us that too.

story:
The cedar beside Écully's town hall grew up in the park of an old horticultural estate, and the Métropole's register calls it one of the oldest in the commune. It is a Cedar of Lebanon, protected as a remarkable tree on Place de la Libération, and the register notes its excellent health.

It does not stand alone. About 30 metres away on the same square, a second protected cedar is an Atlas cedar of the blue-needled form, glauca, which the register picks out for its remarkable habit and development. Side by side, the two show how differently two close relatives can grow on one square.

What the horticultural estate grew, and when the cedars went in, the register does not say. Nobody has published a planting date, so this page gives them no age, only the register's word that the Lebanon cedar is among the commune's oldest.

Both register entries were last updated in May 2016. The most recent street-level photographs at the trees are from February 2021, though a photograph of the square taken in August 2026 shows it as it is today. If you visit Écully, tell us both cedars are still there, and send a photograph of each.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as two cedars about 30 metres apart, one with blue-tinged needles. They stand on Place de la Libération beside Écully's town hall; the Cedar of Lebanon is the one nearer the building.
